Circles And Parallels

CirclesGeometryConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: two circles drawn through a point on a triangle's side meet again, and the line between the two meetings always aims at one fixed spot.
How to play: Drag the points A, B, C and P, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show point names or a hint about why the spot never moves.
Look for the math

A problem from Honsberger's Mathematical Delights hides a very stubborn point. Move P along the side of the triangle and the two circles change size and position, yet the line joining their two meeting points keeps going through exactly the same spot.

The two circles

Pick P on AB. Draw PN parallel to BC until it meets AC at N, and PM parallel to AC until it meets BC at M. Now draw the circumcircle of triangle APN and the circumcircle of triangle BPM. Besides P they meet once more at Q. The logic test checks 736 drawings: P and Q both lie on each circle, N stays on AC, M stays on BC, and the two new lines really are parallel to the sides.

The fixed point

Let X be where the tangents to the circumcircle of ABC at A and at B meet. The page claims that every line PQ passes through this X. The test slides P through 7 positions on each of 15 different triangles: X moves less than a billionth of a unit, and its distance from the drawn line PQ is zero to the same precision. X also makes an isosceles triangle on AB: XA = XB, and the angle at A is angle C (or its supplement when C is obtuse).

Why it must happen

Because PN is parallel to BC, triangles ANP and ABC are scaled copies of one another about A (a homothety). Their circumcircles share the same tangent at A, so XA is tangent to the circle APN. In the same way XB is tangent to the circle BPM. Since XA = XB, X has the same power with respect to both circles: it lies on their radical axis, which for intersecting circles is exactly the common chord PQ. Tick “Hint” to see the circumcircle of ABC and the two tangents that build X.

When the circles touch

The page notes that if the two circles are tangent, their common tangent should take the place of PQ. The port draws that real tangent, through P and perpendicular to the line joining the two circle centres; the test finds tangencies and confirms that this line still goes through X. One difference from the original applet is deliberate: in the tangent case the applet drew the line through P perpendicular to PA instead, and that line misses X. The page's stated theorem wins here.

Try this: tick “Names” and “Hint”, then drag P from one end of AB to the other. Watch the line through P and Q swing around the dark point X without ever leaving it.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
